questions.prompt: Why is visible blame costly in this chapter?
choices: Because public stain can cling to the authority figure who seems to carry the harsh act directly
Because responsibility should always disappear into process
Because direct action is always weak

explanation.direct: Authority can suffer when blame and harshness attach too directly to the same hands that must continue to lead.
explanation.competitive: Right. The residue of visible dirt often sticks to the carrier, not just to the event.

questions.prompt: What do buffers or intermediaries preserve here?

explanation.gentle: Yes. Buffers matter because they can keep the central figure cleaner in public perception.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats distance as a way of preserving usable authority.

questions.prompt: When does clean-hands strategy become reckless scapegoating or loss of control?
choices: When the central figure stays one step removed from visible dirt
When the buffer becomes obvious, unjust, too autonomous, or more politically dangerous than the center
When process carries part of the burden

explanation.gentle: Exactly. The tactic fails when the shield becomes the scandal or the agent escapes governance.
explanation.direct: Distance stops being strategic once it looks abusive or loses control.
explanation.competitive: Right. A buffer that turns into the story destroys the protection it was meant to provide.
